tasks.q: Press Run. The program counts the characters in a word.
brief: Nothing is marked on this one.
Count the letters of otter yourself and check Python agrees.
tasks.fb: len() does the counting for you, however long the text is.

teach.say: A string is a piece of text. len() counts how many characters it holds and hands back a whole number. Spaces count as characters too.

lines: Keep the word otter under the name w.
Count the characters in w and display the number.

tasks.q: What will this program display?
brief: Read every line before you choose.
tasks.fb: Counting starts at 0, so word[0] is the first character and word[1] is the second one.

teach.say: Every character in a string has a position. The first one is at position 0, the second at position 1, and so on. Square brackets ask for one position.

lines: Keep the word milk under the name t.
Display the character at position 0, which is m.
Display the character at position 2, which is l.

tasks.q: Change the program so it displays the last character instead of the first.
brief: Change only the number inside the square brackets.
The word stays stone.
Display exactly: e
tasks.fb: Five characters give positions 0, 1, 2, 3 and 4, so the last one is always one less than the length.

tests.why: The letter s is still coming out. stone has five characters, so its positions are 0 to 4 and the last one is 4.

hint.think: Count the characters of stone, then remember that the first one is at position `0`.

tasks.q: What will this program display?
brief: Count the characters in cat first.
Then work out which position the second print() is asking for.
tasks.fb: The length counts from 1 but the positions count from 0, so the last character sits at len() - 1.

teach.say: A word of three characters has positions 0, 1 and 2. So the last position is always one less than the length, which is written len() - 1. There is no character at position len() at all.

tasks.q: Finish the program so it displays the last character of the word the user types.
brief: The user types in one word.
Replace ____ with the position of the last character.
It has to work for a word of any length.
One line of output.
tasks.fb: w[len(w) - 1] is the last character of any word, short or long.

tests.why: bridge has six characters, so its last position is 5. Replace the ____ with something worked out from len(w).
A word of one character has only position 0, so the first and last character are the same one.
A different length again, so a number written in by hand fails here.

hint.think: Work the position out from the length instead of typing a number in.

teach.say: len(w) - 1 is the last position whatever the word is. A number written in by hand only ever works for words of one length.

tasks.q: Ask the user for one word. Display how many characters it has. Then display its first character on the next line. Then display its last character on the next line.
brief: The user types in one word.
Three lines of output, in that order.
It has to work for a word of only one character.
tasks.fb: len() for the length, w[0] for the first character, w[len(w) - 1] for the last one.
tasks.starter: # The length, the first character, then the last one

tests.why: Six characters, then b, then e. The last position is 5 and not 6.
One character, so the first and the last are the same one. A crash here means a position such as w[5] was written in by hand.
A shorter word, so every line has to be worked out from the word itself.

hint.think: The length comes from len(), and so does the last position.

tasks.q: This program should display the last character of the word. Find the mistake and put it right.
brief: Press Run first and read the error message.
The user types in one word.
Display exactly one character.
tasks.fb: IndexError means a position past the end of the string. The last one is always len() - `1`, and Python offers w[-1] as a short cut for exactly that.

tests.why: IndexError means a position past the end of the string. bridge stops at position 5.
Even a word of one character has no position 1, so the length is always one too far.
Take one off the length and the same line works for every word.

hint.think: The positions stop one short of the length. Which position does len(w) point at?
walk: A word of four characters has positions 0, 1, 2 and 3.
len(w) is 4, and there is no character sitting there.
Take one off before using the length as a position.

teach.say: The length and the last position are not the same number. A word of four characters has its last character at position 3.

tasks.q: Ask the user for a word. Then ask for a position as a whole number. Display the character at that position. Display `"no such position"` instead when the word has no character there.
brief: The user types in two lines: one word, then a whole number.
Positions count from 0 and are never below 0.
Display exactly: no such position
One line of output.
tasks.fb: Comparing the position with len() is what makes one program work for every word.
tasks.starter: # The character at that position, if there is one

tests.why: Position 2 is the third character, because the counting starts at 0.
Position 0 is the first character. An l here means 1 was added to the position somewhere.
planet has six characters, so 5 is the highest position there is. Refusing it means the test was p < len(w) - 1.
Position 6 is one past the end: six characters, last position 5.
A word of one character has only position 0, so compare against the length and never against a number of your own.

hint.think: A word of n characters has positions 0 to n - 1, so compare the position with the length before using it.

tasks.q: Press Run. The program takes two runs of characters out of one word.
brief: Nothing is marked on this one.
Count the characters in each answer and compare it with the two numbers.
tasks.fb: A slice hands back b - a characters, because the end position is left out.

teach.say: A slice takes a run of characters. In w[a:b] the counting starts at position a and stops just before position b, so b itself is left out.

lines: Keep the word anchor under the name w.
Take positions 0, 1 and 2, which gives anc.
Take positions 2, 3 and 4, which gives cho.

tasks.q: What will this program display?
brief: Read every line before you choose.
tasks.fb: w[0:2] gives two characters and w[1:4] gives three, because each slice stops before its second number.

teach.say: The second number in a slice is a stopping point, not the last position taken. Take the first number from the second to know how many characters come back.

tasks.q: Change the program so it displays the first four characters instead of the first two.
brief: Change only the second number.
The word stays harbour.
Display exactly: harb
tasks.fb: Starting at `0` and stopping before `4` gives four characters: positions 0, 1, 2 and 3.

tests.why: ha is still coming out, so the second number was not changed. Four characters are wanted, so the slice stops before position 4.

hint.think: The second number says where to stop, not which position to finish on.

tasks.q: Finish the program so it displays the first three characters of the word the user types.
brief: The user types in one word of at least three characters.
Replace ____ with the two numbers of the slice.
One line of output.
tasks.fb: w[0:3] takes positions 0, 1 and 2, which is three characters.

tests.why: Three characters are wanted, so the slice stops before position 3. harb means it stopped before position 4.
A word of exactly three characters gives all three. ca means the slice stopped one too early.
A different word, so three characters typed in by hand fail here.

hint.think: Start at the very beginning and stop before the fourth character.

teach.say: A slice needs two numbers: where to start and where to stop. w[0:2] starts at the beginning and stops before position 2, so it gives two characters.

tasks.q: Ask the user for one word. Display the word without its first character.
brief: The user types in one word of at least two characters.
One line of output.
Only the first character is left out.
tasks.fb: w[1:len(w)] starts one character in and runs to the end.

tests.why: Start at position 1 so the s is left behind, and stop at the length so nothing else is.
A word of two characters leaves one behind. An empty line means the slice stopped too early.
A different word, so the second number has to come from len(w).

hint.think: Start the slice one position further in and let it run to the end of the word.

tasks.q: This program should display as many characters from the start of the text as the user asks for. Find the mistake and put it right.
brief: Press Run first and read the error message.
The user types in two lines: a line of text, then a whole number.
Display that many characters, counting from the start.
tasks.fb: input() gives text, and a slice needs numbers. int() on the way in is the fix, exactly as in lesson 1.

tests.why: A TypeError here means a slice was given text instead of a number. Cast the typed line with int( ).
One character this time, so the number really does come from what was typed.
The number can be the whole length of the text, which gives all of it back.

hint.think: Look at the data type of the value being used inside the square brackets.

teach.say: input() hands back text every time, even when the user typed digits. A slice needs whole numbers, so the typed line has to be cast with int() first.

tasks.q: Ask the user for a line of text. Display the text without its first and last characters. Display `"nothing inside"` instead when the text has fewer than three characters.
brief: The user types in one line of text, which may be empty.
Display exactly: nothing inside
One line of output.
tasks.fb: A short slice gives an empty string rather than an error, so only a length test can catch a short line.
tasks.starter: # Drop one character from each end

tests.why: Start at position 1 and stop before the last position. tulip# means the last character was never dropped.
Two characters are left in the middle. Getting a means the slice stopped one too early.
Exactly three characters leaves one in the middle, which is the smallest text that has a middle at all.
Two characters leave nothing in the middle, and the slice would quietly give an empty string.
An empty line has no characters at all, so the length has to be checked before anything is taken.

hint.think: A slice that asks for too much hands back an empty string instead of crashing, so the length has to be tested yourself.

tasks.q: Press Run. Look at the third line of output and compare it with the first.
brief: Nothing is marked on this one.
The variable w is displayed last, after both methods have been used on it.
tasks.fb: Both methods hand back a new string. The variable keeps the word it already had.

teach.say: upper() hands back a copy of a string with every letter made capital. lower() hands back a copy with every letter made small. Neither one changes the original.

lines: Keep the word Ferry under the name w.
Display a capital-letter copy of w.
Display a small-letter copy of w.
Display w itself, which still holds the word it started with.

tasks.q: What will this program display?
brief: Read every line before you choose.
tasks.fb: F and f are two different characters, so a == b is False. Lower both and the same words match.

teach.say: A capital letter is not the same character as its small letter, so two words typed differently are not equal. Putting both into the same case first is what makes the comparison fair.

tasks.q: Change the program so capitals are ignored and it displays True.
brief: Change only the last line.
Both words stay exactly as they are.
Display exactly: True
tasks.fb: The two words are only lowered for the comparison. Neither variable is changed by it.

tests.why: False is still coming out, because F and f are two different characters. Put both words into the same case inside the comparison.

hint.think: Both words have to reach the == in the same case.

tasks.q: Finish the program so it displays `"match"` when the two words are the same word, ignoring capitals.
brief: The user types in two words, one on each line.
Replace ____ so both words are compared in the same case.
Display exactly: match or different
tasks.fb: Lower both sides, or upper both sides. What matters is that they match each other.

tests.why: Only the capital H differs, so both words have to reach the == in the same case.
Changing one word only is not enough: both sides need the same treatment.
Two different words already in the same case, so capitals play no part here.
One letter in either case is the smallest version of this test.
An extra s makes them different words. Ignoring capitals does not mean ignoring letters.

hint.think: One side of the == has already been made small. The other side has not.

teach.say: Both sides of the comparison have to be in the same case. Changing only one of them leaves the two words unequal.

tasks.q: Ask the user for a word. Display `"all capitals"` when every letter of the word is a capital. Display `"not all capitals"` when it is not.
brief: The user types in one word.
Display exactly: all capitals or not all capitals
One line of output.
tasks.fb: upper() hands back a copy, and comparing the word with that copy says whether anything changed.
tasks.starter: # Is the word all in capitals?

tests.why: Every letter is already a capital, so the word and its capital copy are the same string.
One capital is not enough: the b and the c change when the copy is made.
No capitals at all, so the capital copy is a different string.
One capital letter on its own is still all capitals.

hint.think: Compare the word with a capital copy of itself.

teach.say: A word is already in capitals when it is the same string as its own capital copy. Comparing a word with w.upper() is how a program finds that out.

tasks.q: This program should display `"match"` when the two words are the same word, ignoring capitals. Find the mistake and put it right.
brief: Press Run first and try the same word twice, once with a capital.
The user types in two words, one on each line.
Display exactly: match or different
tasks.fb: A method's answer has to be stored or used. On its own that line changes nothing at all.
tasks.starter:
a = input()
b = input()
a.lower()
b.lower()
if a == b:
    print("match")
else:
    print("different")

tests.why: The same word with one capital came out as different, so the lowered copies were never used.
Store each copy with an = sign, or lower both words inside the comparison itself.
Two different words stay different, which is why the mistake is easy to miss.

hint.think: lower() hands a new string back. Is anything being done with those two answers?
walk: Lines 3 and 4 each make a small-letter copy.
Nothing stores either copy, so both are thrown away.
The == on line 5 still sees the words exactly as they were typed.

tasks.q: Ask the user for a word. Then ask for a second word. Ignoring capitals, work out which of them comes first alphabetically. Display that word.
brief: The user types in two words, one on each line.
They are never the same word.
A shorter word that starts the other one comes first.
Display the word as the user typed it.
tasks.fb: Compare in one case, display in the other: the words are only lowered for the test, not for the output.
tasks.starter: # Which of the two words comes first alphabetically?

tests.why: l comes before m, so the second word wins. mint here means the comparison was the wrong way round.
Compared as typed, Zebra would win, because every capital has a lower code than every small letter.
The shorter word comes first when one starts the other, because it runs out of letters sooner.
The same pair the other way round, so the answer cannot simply be the first or the second word read.

hint.think: Compare the small-letter versions, but display the word the user typed.

teach.say: < compares two strings character by character. Every capital has a lower code than every small letter, so both words go into the same case before they are compared or the answer depends on how they were typed.

tasks.q: Press Run. The program asks two questions about one line of text.
brief: Nothing is marked on this one.
True and False are the only two answers a test like this can give.
tasks.fb: in answers yes or no. It never says where in the text the word was found.
tasks.starter:
t = "hot soup"
print("soup" in t)
print("cold" in t)

teach.say: word in text is True when the word appears somewhere inside the text. The thing being looked for is written first and the text it is looked for in comes after.

lines: Keep the words hot soup under the name t.
Ask whether soup appears anywhere in t, which it does.
Ask whether cold appears anywhere in t, which it does not.

tasks.q: What will this program display?
brief: Read every line before you choose.
tasks.fb: wet and the space fill positions 0 to 3, so paint starts at 4. A word that is not there gives -1.

teach.say: find() gives the position where the word first appears, counting from 0. When the word is not there at all it gives -1, which is not a position.

tasks.q: Change the program so it displays the position where the word `"kettle"` starts.
brief: Change only the word being looked for.
The line of text stays the same.
Display one number.
tasks.fb: find() reports where its own word starts, so changing the word changes the number.

tests.why: 0 is still coming out, which is where copper starts. copper and the space fill positions 0 to 6, so kettle starts at 7.

hint.think: find() looks for whatever word it is handed.

tasks.q: Finish the program so it displays `"found"` when the word appears in the text.
brief: The user types in two lines: a line of text, then a word to look for.
Replace ____ with the test.
Display exactly: found or missing
tasks.fb: word in text asks whether word appears anywhere inside text, and nothing more than that.

tests.why: tide is right at the start, and in looks anywhere rather than only at the start.
sand is not there at all, so a program that always displays found fails here.
The word is longer than the text, so it cannot be inside it. The order of the two names matters.
A space is a character like any other, so e i really does appear in the middle.

hint.think: Which of the two is being looked for, and which is being looked in?

teach.say: The thing being looked for goes before the word in, and the text being searched goes after it. The other way round asks a different question.

tasks.q: Ask the user for a line of text. Then ask for a word to look for. Display the position where the word starts, counting from 0. Display `"not found"` instead when the word is not there.
brief: The user types in two lines: a line of text, then a word to look for.
Positions count from 0.
Display exactly: not found
One line of output.
tasks.fb: Keep find()'s answer in a variable, test it for `-1`, and display it only when it really is a position.
tasks.starter: # Where in the text does the word start?

tests.why: copper and the space fill positions 0 to 6, so kettle starts at 7. An 8 means the counting started at 1.
A word at the very start is at position 0, and 0 is a real answer.
find() gives -1 when nothing matches, and -1 is not a position, so it has to be tested for.
There are three letter e characters and find() reports only the first one.
The first place aa fits is right at the start, so the answer is 0 and not 1.

hint.think: find() answers both halves of this on its own: a position, or `-1` when there is nothing.

tasks.q: This program should display the position of the word, or `"not found"` when the word is not there. Find the mistake and put it right.
brief: Press Run first and try looking for a word at the very start.
The user types in two lines: a line of text, then a word to look for.
Display exactly: not found
tasks.fb: `0` is the first position, not a failure. Only `-1` means the word is not in the text.
tasks.starter:
text = input()
word = input()
place = text.find(word)
if place > 0:
    print(place)
else:
    print("not found")

tests.why: A word further in already works, which is why the mistake is easy to miss.
copper starts at position 0, so not found here means 0 was treated as a failure.
This is the only case where find() really gives -1.

hint.think: Which answers from find() really mean the word was not there?
walk: Only `-1` means no match at all.
`0` means a match right at the start of the text.
The test on line 4 is sending `0` to the wrong branch.

teach.say: find() gives -1 when there is no match. 0 is a real position: it means the very start of the text.

tasks.q: Ask the user for a line of text. Then ask for a word to look for. Display `"at the start"` when the text begins with the word. Display `"inside"` when the word appears later. Display `"missing"` when it is not there at all.
brief: The user types in two lines: a line of text, then a word to look for.
Display exactly one of: at the start, inside, missing
A word that begins the text counts as `"at the start"` and not as `"inside"`.
tasks.fb: One call to find() and two comparisons sort all three cases out.
tasks.starter: # At the start, further in, or not there at all?

tests.why: is appears in the middle, so the position is neither -1 nor 0.
The text begins with tide, so the position is exactly 0.
The word is not there at all, so find() gives -1.
A single character can be at the start too.
ana appears twice but never at position 0, so where the first match is decides the answer.

hint.think: One number from find() answers all three cases.
walk: Get the position once and keep it in a variable.

tasks.q: Press Run. Every character is stored as a number, and this program shows three of them.
brief: Nothing is marked on this one.
Look at how far apart the codes for a and A are.
tasks.fb: Small a is 97 and capital A is 65, so the gap between the two cases is always 32.

teach.say: Every character is stored as a whole number called its code. ord() gives the code of a character, and chr() turns a code back into its character.

lines: Display the code of the small letter a.
Display the code of the capital letter A.
Display the character whose code is 98.

tasks.q: What will this program display?
brief: Read every line before you choose.
tasks.fb: b is one more than a, and adding 2 to the code of a steps along to c.

teach.say: A code is a whole number, so it can be added to and taken away from. Letters next to each other in the alphabet have codes one apart.

tasks.q: Change the program so it displays the letter before m instead of the letter after it.
brief: Change only the arithmetic.
The letter m stays as it is.
Display exactly: l
tasks.fb: Stepping forwards adds to the code and stepping backwards takes away from it.

tests.why: n is still coming out, so 1 is still being added. Stepping backwards means taking 1 away instead.

hint.think: The letter before has a code one lower.

tasks.q: Finish the program so it displays the code of the character the user types.
brief: The user types in one character.
Replace ____ with the name of the function you need.
Display one number.
tasks.fb: ord() is the one that turns a character into its code.

tests.why: Small d has code 100, and the code comes from the function rather than from a table copied out.
Small a has code 97. A 65 here means a capital A was used instead of what was typed.
Capitals and small letters have different codes, 32 apart, so a and A can never give the same answer.
The digit characters start at 48, so the character 0 is not the number 0.

hint.think: One of the two functions goes from a character to a number.

teach.say: ord() takes one character and hands back its code as a whole number. chr() goes the other way, from a code to a character.

tasks.q: Ask the user for one small letter. Display the code of that letter. Then display the code of its capital letter on the next line.
brief: The user types in one small letter.
Work the second code out from the first one, not with upper().
Two lines of output, both numbers.
tasks.fb: Every capital's code is exactly `32` below its small letter's code.
tasks.starter: # The code of the letter, then the code of its capital

tests.why: a is 97 and A is 65, so the second line is 32 less than the first.
The gap of 32 is the same for every letter of the alphabet.
A letter at the far end of the alphabet works the same way.

hint.think: A capital's code is `32` lower than its small letter's code.

forbid: This one is about the codes, so upper() is not allowed here - the two codes are always 32 apart.

tasks.q: This program should display the character that comes after the one typed. Find the mistake and put it right.
brief: Press Run first and look at what comes out.
The user types in one character.
Display one character, not a number.
tasks.fb: ord() goes from a character to a code, and chr() has to bring it back again.

tests.why: 98 came out instead of b, so the new code was never turned back into a character.
Add 1 to the code first, then hand the answer to chr().
Capitals work the same way: their codes sit next to each other too.

hint.think: A number is coming out. Something has to turn a code back into a character.

tasks.q: Ask the user for one small letter. Work out the next letter of the alphabet. Display that letter. After z the next letter is a.
brief: The user types in one small letter.
After z the answer is a.
One line of output.
tasks.fb: chr() and ord() step along the alphabet, but the end of it has to be handled on purpose.
tasks.starter: # The next letter, with z wrapping round to a

tests.why: d is 100 and 101 is e, which chr() hands back. Leaving chr() out displays 101 instead.
a is 97 and b is 98, so the step forwards is one.
z is 122 and 123 is not a letter at all, so the wrap round to a has to be written yourself.
y is the last letter that needs no wrapping, so treating it as special too would skip z.

hint.think: The codes run out at z, so that one letter has to be dealt with on purpose.

tasks.q: Press Run. The loop takes the word apart one character at a time.
brief: Nothing is marked on this one.
The loop runs once for each character in the string.
tasks.fb: for ch in text: is the easiest way to look at every character of a string in turn.

teach.say: A for loop can run through a string. It hands you one character at a time, starting at the front, and no positions have to be worked out at all.

lines: Take each character of cat in turn and call it ch.
Display the character the loop is holding this time round.

tasks.q: What will this program display?
brief: Read every line before you choose.
tasks.fb: Each time round the loop the old string is used to make the new one, so it grows by one character and one dot.

teach.say: A string can be built up a piece at a time. The variable starts as an empty string, and each time round the loop a longer string is put back into it.

tasks.q: Finish the program so it displays the word with a dash after every character.
brief: The user types in one word.
Replace ____ with the new value for out.
One line of output, with a dash after the last character too.
tasks.fb: out = out + ch + "-" uses the old string to make the new one, which is how a string grows.
tasks.starter:
w = input()
out = ""
for ch in w:
    out = ____
print(out)

tests.why: Three characters give three dashes, one after each. Replace the ____ so out grows every time round the loop.
One character still gets its dash, because the loop runs once.
The dash goes after the character, so the line never starts with one.

hint.think: Join the new character and a dash onto the end of what has been built so far.

tasks.q: What will this program display?
brief: Read every line before you choose.
tasks.fb: ch + out puts each new character in front of everything built so far, so the string comes out backwards.

teach.say: Where the new character is joined on matters. Joining it to the end keeps the order. Joining it in front turns the string round.

tasks.q: This program should display the word backwards. Find the mistake and put it right.
brief: Press Run first and look at what comes out.
The user types in one word.
Build the reversed word yourself, one character at a time.
tasks.fb: rev + ch copies the word. ch + rev builds it backwards.
tasks.starter:
w = input()
rev = ""
for ch in w:
    rev = rev + ch
print(rev)

tests.why: The word came out unchanged, so each character was added to the end instead of the front.
Every character moves, so the first one typed ends up last.
The s moves from the end to the front, which is what shows the word was really turned round.

hint.think: Which end does each new character need to go on?
walk: The loop is right and the output line is right.
Only the line inside the loop builds the string the wrong way round.
Swap the two things being joined there.

forbid: This one asks you to build the reversed word yourself, one character at a time, not with a reversing slice.
This one asks you to build the reversed word yourself, one character at a time, not with reversed().

tasks.q: Ask the user for a line of text. Count how many of its characters are capital letters. Display that count.
brief: The user types in one line of text, which may be empty.
Digits and spaces are not capital letters.
Display one number.
tasks.fb: One counter, one loop, one test inside it. The count is displayed once at the end, not inside the loop.

tests.why: A, L and F are capitals and the rest are not. A 15 here means every character was counted.
No capitals at all, so the counter is set to 0 before the loop and still displayed afterwards.
One capital letter on its own.
M, D and C are capitals. The digit and the space are not letters, so they must not be counted.
An empty line has nothing to count: the loop runs no times at all and the counter is still 0.

hint.think: Start a counter at `0` before the loop and add `1` each time a capital is met.

teach.say: A character is a capital letter when it is different from its own small-letter version. A digit or a space is the same in either case, so this test leaves them out on its own.

lines: Take each character of Ok! in turn.
Display the character, then whether it differs from its own small-letter version.

tasks.q: Ask the user for one word. Display `"palindrome"` when it reads the same both ways once capitals are ignored. Display `"not a palindrome"` when it does not.
brief: The user types in one word.

info.title: Spaces count
info.text: len() counts every character, so a space, a comma and a full stop each add one to the length.

info.title: Open ends
info.text: A slice can leave a number out: word[:3] starts at the beginning and word[3:] runs to the end.

info.title: Nothing is changed
info.text: upper() does not change the original - it hands back a new string. Strings in Python cannot be edited in place.

info.title: Searching fairly
info.text: To search without caring about capitals, lower() both the text and the thing you are looking for before you search.

info.title: Beyond A to Z
info.text: ord() gives a Unicode code point, so it works for letters from any alphabet, not only A to Z.

info.title: Building strings
info.text: Adding to a string makes a brand new one each time. For a long job, collecting the pieces in a list and joining them once is quicker.
